title: Some and Any: Expectations, Questions and Free Choice
summary: Choose some and any according to sentence meaning, not simply whether a question mark appears. Use some in positive statements, offers and expected-yes questions; any in neutral questions, negative contexts and conditions; and any to express unrestricted choice. Use singular agreement and natural singular they with indefinite pronouns.
learningObjectives: Choose some or any in affirmative and negative contexts, including with uncountable and plural nouns.
Distinguish neutral questions with any from offers, requests and expected-yes questions with some.
Use any in conditions and with the meaning it does not matter which, who or where.
Use someone/anyone and similar indefinite pronouns with singular verbs and optional singular they for later reference.

explanation.heading: Some in affirmative statements; any in negative contexts
explanation.body: Some often introduces an unspecified amount or number in an affirmative sentence: some advice, some spare keys. Any commonly appears after not, never and other expressions with negative meaning. It can also occur after without or hardly, even if the whole clause has no not. Neither word gives an exact quantity. Use some or any before a plural countable noun or an uncountable noun, or use somebody, something and similar pronouns instead of a noun.
explanation.example: We have some spare folders, but we do not have any envelopes.

explanation.heading: Questions: whether the speaker expects something
explanation.body: In a neutral question, use any to ask whether a person or thing exists or is available, without assuming the answer. Some is natural when offering or asking for something, or when the question suggests the speaker expects the thing or person to be there. The difference is about intention and expectation, not a ban on some in questions. Keep the context clear when choosing between them.
explanation.example: Could you spare some time to review this draft?

explanation.heading: Any after if and in possible situations
explanation.body: Use any, anyone, anybody, anything or anywhere in clauses introduced by if: If you have any concerns, call us. Similar meanings appear in general promises or instructions about possible events, even without the word if. Any introduces the possibility without claiming that the thing exists. Someone can appear in an if-clause when the speaker has a particular person in mind, so meaning still matters.
explanation.example: If anyone notices an error in the timetable, they should report it.

explanation.heading: Any as unrestricted choice
explanation.body: Any may mean that every option is acceptable: you can choose any colour from this range. Anyone can mean every person who meets the stated condition, and anywhere can indicate freedom to choose a place. This differs from some, which points to an unspecified but limited person, thing or place. In questions about preferences, anything can express that the speaker has no particular preference.
explanation.example: You may reserve any available desk; none is assigned to a particular visitor.

explanation.heading: Indefinite pronouns and singular they
explanation.body: Someone, somebody, anyone and anybody are grammatically singular: someone is, not someone are; anyone needs, not anyone need. To refer back without specifying gender, English commonly uses they, them and their, even though the indefinite pronoun takes a singular verb. Something and anything refer to things, and somewhere and anywhere refer to places. Choose the ending that matches the meaning.
explanation.example: Someone has left their headphones in the recording booth.

left.label: Open question with any
left.example: Do you have any questions about the schedule?
left.note: The speaker checks whether questions exist, without assuming they do.

right.label: Offer using some
right.example: Would you like some help with the registration form?
right.note: The speaker offers help expected to be available.

comparisons.title: An unspecified option versus free choice

left.label: Some: one unspecified destination
left.example: Let’s meet somewhere quiet after class.
left.note: The speaker wants a quiet location, but has not chosen one.

right.label: Any: unrestricted choice
right.example: We can meet anywhere in this building.
right.note: Any location in the stated range is acceptable.

left.label: Someone: an unidentified person
left.example: Someone is waiting to speak to the organiser.
left.note: An actual but unidentified person is waiting.

right.label: Anyone: no restriction
right.example: Anyone with a ticket can enter the exhibition.
right.note: Every person meeting the ticket condition is eligible.

examples.sentence: The technician asked for some additional details about the fault.
examples.note: Some suggests a quantity of details that is not specified.

examples.sentence: I never carry any cash when I cycle to work.
examples.note: Any is natural in a negative-meaning statement with never.

examples.sentence: Are you expecting someone from the delivery company?
examples.note: Someone reflects the speaker’s suspicion that a visitor is expected.

examples.sentence: If you find anything damaged, photograph it before unpacking.
examples.note: Anything is appropriate in a possible condition.

examples.sentence: Any participant may leave feedback anonymously after the workshop.
examples.note: Any expresses that no participant is excluded by the rule.

examples.sentence: Anybody who wants a copy should leave their email address.
examples.note: Anybody is singular for wants; their refers back naturally without choosing a gender.

commonMistakes.incorrect: There is a some useful guidance on the noticeboard.
commonMistakes.correct: There is some useful guidance on the noticeboard.
commonMistakes.why: Some already determines the uncountable noun guidance; do not add a before it.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Do you have a any comments on the new policy?
commonMistakes.correct: Do you have any comments on the new policy?
commonMistakes.why: Any is a determiner before the plural noun comments, so a is unnecessary and incorrect.

commonMistakes.incorrect: Anyone who needs access are welcome to apply.
commonMistakes.correct: Anyone who needs access is welcome to apply.
commonMistakes.why: Anyone is grammatically singular, so use is, even when it refers to people generally.

commonMistakes.incorrect: If anybody want a receipt, tell the cashier.
commonMistakes.correct: If anybody wants a receipt, tell the cashier.
commonMistakes.why: Anybody takes a singular present-simple verb, wants.

studyTips: For each question, decide whether it is neutral, a genuine offer/request or a question expecting confirmation before choosing some or any.
Rewrite three choices as free-choice sentences using any, anyone and anywhere; make the available options explicit.
Practise the pattern anyone needs … they can …, noticing singular agreement in the first clause and natural they in the next.

exercises.prompt: We need ___ extra chairs for the seminar, so I will ask the caretaker.
exercises.feedback: The speaker affirms that an unspecified number of extra chairs are needed, so some is natural.

exercises.prompt: There were hardly ___ visitors in the gallery before noon.
exercises.feedback: Hardly has nearly negative meaning, so hardly any visitors means almost no visitors.

exercises.prompt: You may select ___ of the available dates; the trainer can attend them all.
exercises.feedback: Any of the available dates means there is no restriction on which date is selected.

exercises.prompt: A host is offering refreshments to arriving guests: “Would you like ___ tea?”
exercises.feedback: Some is natural in a polite offer when tea is available.

exercises.prompt: We have ___ spare notebooks in the cupboard if you need one. (use some or any; positive statement)
acceptedAnswers: some
exercises.feedback: Some indicates an unspecified number of notebooks known to be available.

exercises.prompt: The receptionist has not received ___ messages for you today. (use some or any; neutral negative)
acceptedAnswers: any
exercises.feedback: Not ... any describes the absence of messages without selecting a particular subset.

exercises.prompt: If ___ calls while I am away, please take their name. (one indefinite pronoun meaning any person)
acceptedAnswers: anyone
anybody
exercises.feedback: Anyone or anybody introduces a possible caller; their can refer back to that person.

exercises.prompt: Every seat is free. You can sit ___ in the front row. (one free-choice place word)
acceptedAnswers: anywhere
exercises.feedback: Anywhere signals that no seat in the stated row is restricted.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: I bought a some coloured paper for the display.
acceptedAnswers: I bought some coloured paper for the display.
exercises.feedback: Some determines the uncountable noun paper in this context; a cannot occur before some.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Does a anyone here know how to reset this clock?
acceptedAnswers: Does anyone here know how to reset this clock?
exercises.feedback: Anyone is an indefinite pronoun and cannot be preceded by the article a.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: Someone are waiting near the reception desk.
acceptedAnswers: Someone is waiting near the reception desk.
exercises.feedback: Someone is singular, so it takes is despite its indefinite meaning.

exercises.prompt: Correct the sentence: If anybody need an accessible seat, they can ask the steward.
acceptedAnswers: If anybody needs an accessible seat, they can ask the steward.
exercises.feedback: Anybody takes needs in the if-clause; they can still refer back to that person.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say one affirmative sentence from these exact facts: we / have / some / spare batteries / in the drawer. Use the present simple.
acceptedAnswers: We have some spare batteries in the drawer.
speakingExercises.feedback: Some introduces an unspecified positive quantity of batteries.

speakingExercises.prompt: Make this affirmative statement negative without changing its other words: “The shop has some postcards.” Begin with “The shop”.
acceptedAnswers: The shop doesn't have any postcards.
The shop does not have any postcards.
speakingExercises.feedback: Use any in the negative and the base verb have after does not.

speakingExercises.prompt: Ask a neutral yes/no question using these exact words: the library / have / any / quiet rooms. Begin with “Does”.
acceptedAnswers: Does the library have any quiet rooms?
speakingExercises.feedback: A neutral existence question naturally uses any.

speakingExercises.prompt: A guest asks for water. Offer it with one question using exactly: “Would you like” and “some water”.
acceptedAnswers: Would you like some water?
speakingExercises.feedback: Some is the natural choice for offering an available drink.

speakingExercises.prompt: There are three empty tables, and all are acceptable. Say one sentence using: you / can / choose / any table.
acceptedAnswers: You can choose any table.
speakingExercises.feedback: Any table expresses unrestricted choice among the tables.

speakingExercises.prompt: Your teammate may need help later. Give this instruction as one sentence beginning “If” and using: anyone / need / help / call me. Use the present simple in the condition.
acceptedAnswers: If anyone needs help, call me.
speakingExercises.feedback: Anyone takes the singular verb needs, followed by the instruction call me.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say exactly two sentences. First: someone / wait / outside (present continuous). Second: they / have / a parcel (present simple).
acceptedAnswers: Someone is waiting outside. They have a parcel.
Someone's waiting outside. They have a parcel.
speakingExercises.feedback: Someone takes is; they is natural when referring back to the unidentified visitor.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct the determiner in the following sentence and say the complete corrected sentence: “We have a some new equipment in the workshop.”
acceptedAnswers: We have some new equipment in the workshop.
speakingExercises.feedback: Do not place a before some with the uncountable noun equipment.

listeningExercises.prompt: What does the speaker believe about the conference room?
choices: It is available for immediate use.
listeningExercises.feedback: Someone and the audible conversation show that the speaker expects a person to be inside.
listeningExercises.audioText: I think someone's using the conference room because I can hear two people speaking inside.

listeningExercises.prompt: What information is the speaker asking for?
choices: Whether at least one reply has arrived.
listeningExercises.feedback: Any replies asks neutrally whether replies exist, without assuming they do.
listeningExercises.audioText: Did you receive any replies to your invitation? I have not heard from the guests yet.

listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word noun phrase heard immediately after “isn’t”.
acceptedAnswers: any milk
listeningExercises.feedback: Isn’t any milk expresses that the fridge has no milk left.
listeningExercises.audioText: There isn't any milk in the office fridge, so I'll pick some up on my way back.

listeningExercises.prompt: What restriction applies to the participant’s choice?
choices: Only the earliest workshop is available.
Registration is limited to two workshops.
There is no restriction among the four sessions.
listeningExercises.feedback: Any of the four and every session has places mean all four are possible choices.
listeningExercises.audioText: You can register for any of the four workshops. Every session still has places available.

listeningExercises.prompt: Who is eligible to collect a printed timetable?
listeningExercises.feedback: If anyone needs ... they can makes the offer available to every person who meets the condition.
listeningExercises.audioText: If anyone needs a printed timetable, they can collect one at the information desk.

choices: Offering a drink that is available.
Asking whether the listener bought water.
Explaining why the jug is empty.
listeningExercises.feedback: Would you like some ... is an offer, supported by the newly filled jug.
listeningExercises.audioText: Would you like some chilled water? I filled a jug just before you arrived.

listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two words heard immediately after “notice”.
acceptedAnswers: anything unusual
listeningExercises.feedback: Anything unusual refers to a possible unexpected observation.
listeningExercises.audioText: Please tell the supervisor if you notice anything unusual during the final equipment check.

listeningExercises.prompt: Type the two-word phrase at the beginning of the recording.
acceptedAnswers: Anyone can
listeningExercises.feedback: Anyone can expresses permission without restricting the person.
listeningExercises.audioText: Anyone can attend the evening lecture, and there is no need to register beforehand.
